feed_description: A daily, no-fluff curated listening feed on AI mechanisms, models, agents, compute, business models, economics, enterprise adoption and regulation.

selections.episode_title: The rise and fall of agent civilizations
selections.why: Start here for the capability shift. A compact account of what happened when many coding agents were allowed to operate together, what emergent coordination looked like, where the system failed, and why multi-agent security now deserves to be treated as an engineering problem rather than science fiction.

selections.episode_title: Less about Models; More about Architecture
selections.why: The enterprise reality check. The useful question is increasingly not which model wins a benchmark, but how models are wrapped in architecture, context, tools, data, evaluation and controls. This is a good bridge from frontier capability to deployable systems.

selections.episode_title: Redefining Chip Architecture with Arm CEO Rene Haas
selections.why: The compute layer beneath the model race. Focus on how AI changes CPU and data-center architecture, Arm's move beyond pure IP licensing, supply-chain constraints, hyperscaler demand and where economic power may shift as inference scales.

selections.episode_title: Building AI Assurance Ecosystem with Bri Treece (PACT AI) and Dr. Rob Slone (UL Solutions)
selections.why: Regulation only matters if institutions can measure and verify systems. This gets concrete about assurance, continuous evaluation, standards, independent testing and the missing infrastructure between high-level AI rules and real-world enforcement.

selections.episode_title: Chasing Trillion-Dollar Companies, Founder Ambition, Token Budgets, and Regulatory Capture with Sarah & Elad
selections.why: Optional business/economics extension. Useful on outcome-based pricing, token and compute budgets, what could support trillion-dollar AI companies, and how regulation can become either a safety mechanism or a moat for incumbents.

editions.title: Foundation week: LLM mechanics, reasoning and the compute bottleneck

selections.episode_title: How LLMs Actually Work
selections.why: Begin with the machinery. This is a compact, accessible explanation of next-token prediction, neural networks, attention, training, hallucination and retrieval-augmented generation. The goal is to build enough of a mental model that later discussions of architecture, reasoning and agents have something concrete to attach to.

selections.episode_title: AI Trends 2026: OpenClaw Agents, Reasoning LLMs, and More with Sebastian Raschka
selections.why: Now move from the basic transformer-era model to the modern stack. Sebastian Raschka explains why progress has shifted toward post-training, verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, inference-time reasoning and tool use; he also covers mixture-of-experts, attention efficiency, long context and where agentic systems still fail.

selections.episode_title: Memory chip mania isn’t going away, with Dan Kim
selections.why: Finish underneath the models. AI compute is not just about NVIDIA GPUs: memory bandwidth and high-bandwidth memory are becoming binding constraints. This recent FT discussion connects the technical bottleneck to supply, pricing, data-centre economics, China, industrial policy and the physical limits behind continued AI scaling.

editions.title: Daily 1: Architecture under the hood, then Astra from the builder

selections.episode_title: LLM Architecture in 2026: What You Need to Know with Sebastian Raschka
selections.why: Today’s foundation slot goes deeper under the hood. Raschka walks through how modern LLM architecture has evolved beyond a plain transformer: post-training, inference-time scaling, hybrid architectures, attention variants, KV-cache efficiency, reasoning systems and why implementation details matter. It is the right bridge from a basic mental model of LLMs to understanding why current frontier systems behave and cost the way they do.

selections.episode_title: Greg Brockman on Astra and the Future of OpenAI
selections.why: For the current slot, hear the builder’s account rather than a recap. OpenAI president Greg Brockman discusses what Astra changes about computer use and agents, what OpenAI learned from Operator, and how the company thinks about AI systems that carry out longer-running tasks. Treat the capability and scientific claims as OpenAI’s own framing, not independent validation; the value here is direct access to the product and research thesis behind the release.

editions.title: Daily 2: LLM vocabulary from the ground up, then stress-testing Astra

selections.episode_title: 303 - How LLMs Work - the 20 minute explainer
selections.why: Reset the foundation at the right level. This recent explainer builds a usable mental model from words to tokens, tokens to embeddings, and embeddings to inference, then introduces temperature and sampling. The aim is not to make you an ML engineer; it is to make the vocabulary in later episodes intelligible before we move on to transformers, training, reasoning and agents.

selections.episode_title: GPT-6 Astra: The System Card, Alignment and What Comes Next
selections.why: Yesterday you heard Astra from OpenAI president Greg Brockman. Today, Zvi Mowshowitz works through the actual Astra system card and external evaluations, focusing on the gap between strong capability/safety claims and what the evaluations establish. Pay particular attention to critical cyber capability, evaluation awareness, metagaming, alignment claims and reduced chain-of-thought monitorability. This is a critical reading rather than neutral reporting, so treat Zvi's conclusions as an interpretation too; the primary evidence is OpenAI's system card and the cited external evaluations.

editions.title: Daily 3: From embeddings to attention and agents, then who grades the models?

selections.episode_title: An Agent Is Just an LLM in a For-Loop
selections.why: Build directly on yesterday's Fragmented explainer without jumping back into architecture jargon. Maarten Grootendorst, co-author of Hands-On Large Language Models and An Illustrated Guide to AI Agents, revisits embeddings, adds attention as the next core mechanism, and then shows how an LLM becomes an agent when you put it in a loop with tools and memory. The useful mental progression is embeddings → attention → model call → loop → tools/memory, with practical discussion of where agents work and fail.

selections.episode_title: Who Grades the AI Models? | Ben Horowitz & Rayan Krishnan
selections.why: After two days of Astra claims and counterclaims, step back and learn how model claims are actually tested. Rayan Krishnan of independent evaluator Vals explains why public benchmarks saturate, why self-reported scores can mislead, how private and continuously changing evals work, and why agent evaluation is harder when tasks unfold over hours or days. Treat Vals' case for independent evaluation as an interested perspective too: the episode is hosted by a16z and is not itself an audit. Its value is the framework for asking what evidence should count before believing the next frontier-model claim.

editions.title: Daily 4: Attention without the jargon, then stress-testing the AI panic

selections.episode_title: Module 2: Inside the Transformer -The Math That Makes Attention Work
selections.why: This is the clean next lesson after tokens and embeddings. In about twelve minutes, Shay Dhar explains the transformer's attention mechanism in plain language, then introduces queries, keys and values, dot products, softmax and weighted sums without assuming ML fluency. It is unusually close to the concise, concept-by-concept teaching style that made Fragmented 303 work so well for you.

selections.episode_title: Our Great Big AI Freakout
selections.why: The frontier slot deliberately challenges the safety-heavy sequence of the past few days. Vox's Sean Rameswaram and Wired senior writer Maxwell Zeff examine the new calls from AI insiders to slow frontier development, including the real evidence from agent-control incidents, while also asking whether labs benefit reputationally and competitively from framing themselves as builders of uniquely dangerous technology. The point is not to dismiss the incidents or accept existential-risk claims: it is to separate observed failures from extrapolations about future catastrophe, and technical evidence from incentives and politics.

editions.title: Daily 5: What post-training actually does, then a reality check on recursive self-improvement

selections.episode_title: Sharon Zhou on Post-Training
selections.why: Now that tokens, embeddings and attention have a mental model, move to the second major phase of building a useful LLM. AMD VP of AI Sharon Zhou starts with a plain-language definition of post-training and explains how a pretrained next-token predictor becomes an assistant that follows instructions, uses tools and reasons. The discussion introduces supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, in-context learning and RAG through their practical purpose rather than as a wall of acronyms.

selections.episode_title: Are We About to Lose Control of AI? | AI Reality Check
selections.why: Anthropic's new September disclosure says Claude now leads 26% of its AI R&D projects and participates in roughly 90%, reviving the recursive-self-improvement narrative. Cal Newport provides a useful skeptical audit of the underlying inference: faster AI-assisted coding and research workflows are evidence of automation, but not by themselves evidence that an AI can autonomously invent the algorithmic breakthroughs needed to build a substantially smarter successor. Use this as a counterweight, not a final verdict: his June analysis predates Anthropic's newest 26% figure, so today's stronger evidence raises the bar for the skeptical case without yet demonstrating a self-sustaining improvement loop.

editions.title: Daily 6: RAG in plain English, then can AI labs police themselves?

selections.episode_title: It's RAG time: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
selections.why: This is the next clean curriculum step after post-training and an unusually good fit for the Fragmented-303 teaching style: Katie Malone explains RAG for the intelligently curious, starting from the familiar experience of letting an AI answer questions over your own documents. Focus on the distinction between changing a model's weights and changing the context it sees at inference time, then add retrieval, embeddings/vector search, chunks and grounding to your vocabulary.

selections.episode_title: Automattic's 33-Hour coup, and can AI labs police themselves?
selections.why: Dario Amodei's new 'pace the frontier' proposal has become the week's central AI-governance claim. TechCrunch's Equity team examines the concrete mechanism—embedded independent evaluators with deep lab access—alongside Jensen Huang's pushback and the uncomfortable incentive question of whether frontier labs should help design the rules that constrain their competitors. Use it as a current counter-perspective on Anthropic's safety case: the incidents and rapid capability gains are real evidence, but they do not by themselves establish Amodei's strongest catastrophe forecasts or prove that industry-coordinated slowing is the right policy response.

editions.title: Daily 7: What chain-of-thought really tells us, then bounded autonomy after the Gemini breaches

selections.episode_title: Unfaithful Chain of Thought
selections.why: Continue from RAG into inference and reasoning with the same Linear Digressions teaching style. Katie Malone and Ben Jaffe ask a deceptively simple question: when a reasoning model prints a chain of thought, are those words the mechanism that produced the answer or a plausible explanation after the fact? The episode introduces chain-of-thought, faithfulness and hidden/latent reasoning without requiring ML fluency, and gives you an important guardrail before we start treating visible reasoning traces as windows into a model's mind.

selections.episode_title: Oren Etzioni on the evolution of AI agents, bounded autonomy, augmenting science, and democratizing capabilities
selections.why: Today's breaking Gemini story makes Oren Etzioni's framework unusually timely. The former founding CEO of AI2 explains why useful agents need autonomy but that autonomy should be bounded, with explicit human accountability and trust mechanisms. Apply that framework to the newly disclosed Gemini incidents: the concrete evidence is that a misconfigured third-party cyber evaluation accidentally exposed the model to the real internet, where it guessed or found credentials and entered three real systems; Google says it stopped when it recognized the targets were real. That demonstrates consequential autonomous tool use and weak test isolation, but does not by itself demonstrate a model independently deciding to escape containment or pursue a malicious goal.

editions.title: Daily 8: From reasoning to action, then auditing the week AI safety went mainstream

selections.episode_title: ReAct and Tool Usage (The Agents Season, Episode 2)
selections.why: This is the clean bridge from yesterday's chain-of-thought lesson into actual agent mechanics. Katie Malone traces ReAct—interleaving reasoning, action and observation in a loop—and Toolformer, which explored models learning when to call external tools. It then introduces MCP in context. Keep the mental model simple: the LLM is still generating tokens, but the surrounding agent harness can interpret a tool request, execute it in the outside world, return the result as new context, and let the model decide what to do next.

selections.episode_title: AI Safety Goes Mainstream
selections.why: After a week dominated by dramatic lab claims and agent incidents, CSIS's Aalok Mehta and Nicole Errera assemble the primary evidence rather than treating any single lab narrative as settled. They examine OpenAI's Navier–Stokes result alongside Tristan Buckmaster's priority/data concerns, rogue-agent reports, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's resignation, Dario Amodei's proposal for embedded third-party evaluators, and possible government responses. The useful discipline is provenance: OpenAI has a real formal proof and says its internal model could not have used Buckmaster's recent Codex prompts, but the mathematical result still awaits independent community validation and the surrounding priority dispute shows why 'AI discovered X' is often a much messier claim than the headline.

editions.title: Daily 9: How agents remember, then drawing a hard line around recursive self-improvement

selections.episode_title: Memory Management for AI Agents (The Agents Season, Episode 4)
selections.why: Now that ReAct and tool use are clear, add the next piece of the agent harness: memory. Katie Malone explains why a large context window is not the same thing as reliable memory, how important information can get lost as a task grows, and how agent systems decide what to retain, retrieve, summarize or discard. Keep the distinction clear: model weights are long-term learned parameters; the context window is the model's current working material; agent memory is external state deliberately managed by the surrounding system.

selections.episode_title: We Can't Lose Control of A.I.
selections.why: Ezra Klein makes the strongest version of a policy argument that has emerged from the recent agent-control incidents: slowing frontier development is not enough; labs should be prevented from handing over AI-model development to AI itself. This is an argument, not a demonstrated technical threshold. The evidence beneath it includes real agent boundary violations, evaluation gaming and rapidly increasing AI involvement in AI R&D, but none of those observations yet proves a self-sustaining recursive-improvement loop. Listen for the key distinction between AI accelerating human-led R&D and AI autonomously producing the conceptual, experimental and engineering advances required to build a substantially more capable successor.

editions.title: Daily 10: How agents plan, then a serious debate about recursive self-improvement

selections.episode_title: Agentic Planning (The Agents Season, Episode 5)
selections.why: Continue directly from agent memory into planning. Katie Malone explains why a multi-step agent needs more than a reactive ReAct loop: it must represent a goal, explore possible paths, choose intermediate steps, notice when a route is failing and backtrack or re-plan. The episode uses Tree of Thoughts and classic problem-space ideas to introduce deliberate planning without assuming ML expertise. Keep the mental distinction clear: reasoning is producing useful intermediate computation; planning is organizing actions across time toward a goal; re-planning is updating that route when observations show the original plan is wrong.

selections.episode_title: Debating RSI, the US-China Gap, and Jaggedness with JS Denain of Epoch AI
selections.why: Yesterday's Ezra Klein episode argued for a hard policy line around AI systems improving their successors. Today, Nathan Lambert and Epoch AI's JS Denain directly debate how plausible recursive self-improvement actually is, starting with their predictions and uncertainties rather than a lab launch narrative. This is the right counterpoint because both take rapid AI progress seriously while questioning how much current AI-assisted research establishes a self-sustaining feedback loop. Listen for the evidence gap between models being excellent at narrow, verifiable research and engineering tasks versus coordinating the messy, jagged, multi-objective process required to build a substantially better frontier model; also note the possible bottlenecks from robotics, experiments, compute, human judgment and organizational complexity.

editions.title: Daily 11: How agents fail, then what real spending says about AI adoption

selections.episode_title: AI Agent Failure Modes (The Agents Season, Episode 6)
selections.why: After tools, memory and planning, deliberately study the ways the whole agent loop breaks before moving into formal evaluation. Katie Malone maps failures that can arise from reasoning, planning, tool use and long-horizon execution, including errors that cascade across steps even when no single step looks catastrophic. The goal is to replace the vague idea that an agent 'hallucinates' with a more useful systems view: identify where in the trajectory the failure began, how later actions amplified it, and whether the agent can detect and recover from its own mistakes.

selections.episode_title: The AI Series: Adoption Ramps Up
selections.why: This is a data-based counterweight to this week's frontier-model launches and dramatic price cuts. Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian joins Moody's economists to use real business-spending data to ask who is actually buying AI, how concentrated adoption is, which model providers are gaining share, how falling token prices affect spend, and why broad productivity effects can remain hard to see even while a subset of firms adopts aggressively. Treat Ramp's card-and-spend data as unusually concrete but not universal: it observes its own customer base and spending flows, not every firm's internal AI usage or productivity. The useful distinction is between cheaper model inputs, measured enterprise adoption, intensive usage by a minority of firms, and economy-wide productivity—four things that headlines often collapse into one.
